Websitemodelcontextprotocol.io Relationship between MCP host, MCP clients and MCP servers The Model Context Protocol (MCP) is an open standard and open-source framework introduced by Anthropic in November 2024 to standardize the way artificial intelligence (AI) systems like large language models (LLMs) integrate and share data with external tools, systems, and data sources.[1] MCP provides a standardized interface for reading files, executing functions, and handling contextual prompts.[2] Following its announcement, the protocol was adopted by major AI providers, including OpenAI and Google DeepMind.[3][4]
Background
[edit]
MCP was announced by Anthropic in November 2024 as an open standard[5] for connecting AI assistants to data systems such as content repositories, business management tools, and development environments.[6] The protocol was created at Anthropic by engineers David Soria Parra and Justin Spahr-Summers.[6] It aims to address the challenge of information silos and legacy systems.[6] Before MCP, developers often had to build custom connectors for each data source or tool, resulting in what Anthropic described as an "N×M" data integration problem.[6][7]
Earlier stop-gap approaches—such as OpenAI's 2023 "function-calling" API and the ChatGPT plug-in framework—solved similar problems but required vendor-specific connectors.[7] MCP re-uses the message-flow ideas of the Language Server Protocol (LSP).[8]
In December 2025, Anthropic donated the MCP to the Agentic AI Foundation (AAIF), a directed fund under the Linux Foundation, co-founded by Anthropic, Block and OpenAI, with support from other companies.[9] Later that month, Anthropic also published Agent Skills, a companion open standard for packaging task-specific instructions and resources that AI agents load on demand, following the same open-standard approach as MCP.[10]
Features
[edit]
MCP defines a standardized framework for integrating AI systems with external data sources and tools.[2] MCP enables applications such as querying structured databases with plain language in the field of natural language data access.[8]
The protocol distinguishes between MCP hosts, MCP clients and MCP servers. An MCP host is typically an AI agent that interacts with an LLM and requires services from one or more MCP servers. For each of these MCP servers, the MCP host will create a dedicated MCP client that communicates with that server. Client and host will typically run on the same machine, while the MCP servers may be local or remote.[11]
Each server provides one or more tools or resources. Example tools are: access to a database, calculators, access to code repositories etc.; a resource might be a certain FAQ document. The MCP client asks its server for a list of tools and resources the server provides; the server replies with a natural-language description of the capabilities of each tool and the expected format to call the tool. This information is given to the LLM; if it requires the services of one of these tools, the MCP host will instruct the relevant MCP client to call the tool. The MCP server performs the tool action and returns the results, which the MCP host then injects into the LLM conversation.[11] Client and server communicate using the JSON-RPC 2.0 transport protocol.[8]
The protocol was released with software development kits (SDKs) in programming languages including Python, TypeScript, C# and Java and examples of MCP server implementations.[8][12]
The protocol is used in AI-assisted software development tools. Integrated development environments (IDEs), coding platforms such as Replit, and code intelligence tools like Sourcegraph have adopted MCP to grant AI coding assistants real-time access to project context.[5]
MCP Apps is an official extension to the Model Context Protocol built on mcp-ui. While the base MCP specification is restricted to text and structured data, MCP Apps standardizes the delivery of interactive user interfaces—such as dashboards, forms, and data visualizations—from MCP servers to host applications like Claude and ChatGPT.[13]
Adoption
[edit]
In March 2025, OpenAI officially adopted the MCP, after having integrated the standard across its products, including the ChatGPT desktop app.[3][2] In September 2025, OpenAI added support for MCP to ChatGPT apps. This allows for third-party access inside ChatGPT.[14]
MCP can be integrated with Microsoft Semantic Kernel, and Azure OpenAI.[15] MCP servers can be deployed to Cloudflare.[16]
In April 2026, the AAIF held the MCP Dev Summit North America in New York City, drawing approximately 1,200 attendees.[17] That same month, Salesforce's Headless 360 platform began routing customer and agent interactions via MCP; in late May, Salesforce reported 4.5 million MCP calls had been processed since launch.[18][19]
By mid-2026, more than 10,000 MCP servers had reportedly been deployed in production, with the protocol's SDKs downloaded over 97 million times per month.[20]
2026-07-28 revision
[edit]
On July 28, 2026, MCP's maintainers finalized a major revision of the specification, described by Anthropic technical staff member David Soria Parra as the most substantial change to the protocol since the addition of authorization.[20] The revision removes protocol-level session tracking, making MCP stateless at the protocol layer: information about protocol version, client identity, and capabilities is instead carried in a _meta parameter with each request.[20] The change brings MCP's request model closer to that of Anthropic's own Claude Messages API.[20]
The revision also deprecated several features that had seen limited use, including sampling (allowing a server to request a completion from the client's model) and roots (allowing clients to indicate relevant file-system locations to a server); deprecated features remain functional for a minimum of twelve months.[20] Some previously core functionality, such as the Tasks feature for long-running operations, was moved out of the base protocol and into optional extensions.[20] Not all of the changes are backward compatible, and servers implementing the new revision may not interoperate with older clients without a compatibility layer.[20]
Reception
[edit]
The Verge reported that MCP addresses a growing demand for AI agents that are contextually aware and capable of pulling from diverse sources.[5]
In April 2025, security researchers released an analysis that concluded there are multiple outstanding security issues with MCP, including prompt injection[21] and poisoned tools that allow for data exfiltration through other connected tools.[22]
MCP has been likened to OpenAPI, a similar specification that aims to describe APIs.[23][24]

Notify Me Given the pace of AIs evolution, there’s a massive shift in how organizations leverage it. What started with enterprises focusing on deploying independent AI agents has now evolved to multiple autonomous agents working in synchrony to complete complex tasks and automate unstructured workflows. Multi-agent collaboration is a key necessity, and the focus is shifting to standard protocols that enable agents to communicate, coordinate, and act independently with minimal human intervention. The question is no longer “Can we implement AI agents?” but rather “How to enable AI agents to collaborate?” The MCP (Model Context Protocol) and A2A (Agent-to-Agent protocol) are key enablers in this regard.
MCP provides the structure for contextual understanding and data connectivity, while the A2A protocol establishes the coordination layer through which autonomous agents communicate and achieve shared goals. The Need for Protocol Standardization for Multi-Agent AI Systems
Gartner forecasts that by 2026, nearly every business application will have AI assistants, with 40% integrating task-specific agents within the following year. It’s a significant rise from under just 5% in 2025. As adoption accelerates, so does the complexity of making these AI agents interact and collaborate effectively. Multi-agent collaboration presents multiple challenges. Different vendors use varied frameworks, data formats, and communication methods to build and execute agents. Without standardized protocols, each integration would require custom development work. Protocol standardization fulfills three critical enterprise needs: Interoperability across diverse systems. Scalability without exponential integration complexity. Security through controlled data access patterns. Unlock business value through effective multi-agent AI systems

Architecture and Implementation Benefits
As BCG research puts it, MCP functions as a “USB-C port for AI agents”, a standardized link that significantly reduces the headaches of connecting large language models to tools and data. The Model Context Protocol (MCP) is built on a client–server architecture similar to the Language Server Protocol (LSP). In simple terms, it creates a structured way for large language models (LLMs) to connect with external tools and data sources. The host application, powered by the LLM, includes an MCP client that serves as a bridge to MCP servers, each offering specific capabilities, such as retrieving data, running functions, or integrating with enterprise systems. These interactions are facilitated by communication layers such as Standard Input/Output (STDIO) and Hypertext Transfer Protocol with Server-Sent Events (HTTP+SSE), enabling smooth, secure, and real-time collaboration between AI systems and external resources.
Figure 1: MCP Architecture in a nutshell MCP is significant because it directly addresses a problem that AI agents present for most organizations: interconnectivity. Here are some reasons why MCP is becoming the standard for communication between AI applications, AI agents, and data sources:
MCP uses a standardized protocol as a universal interface between AI models and enterprise tools, eliminating the need for custom connectors in every new system. Manages context and streamlines the flow of relevant information, including memory, prior outputs, and tool results, so agents operate with the proper context at the right time. By implementing MCP, organizations gain advantages in modularity and adaptability, making integrations valuable, reusable assets instead of temporary fixes. The protocol is model-agnostic, ensuring that both current and future AI investments adapt seamlessly to changing enterprise environments and minimize disruptions when integrating new tools or data sources. Employs JSON-RPC 2.0 over stdio or Server-Sent Events (SSE), supporting both lightweight synchronous tasks and asynchronous, event-driven workflows. Looking for MCP use cases for agentic AI?

Agent-to-Agent (A2A) Protocol: Enabling Multi-Agent Collaboration The Agent-to-Agent (A2A) Protocol establishes a common framework that allows autonomous AI agents to collaborate securely and efficiently.. The A2A protocol operates on a client–remote agent model. A client agent starts the process and delegates work to the remote agent by identifying collaborators via a structured “agent card”. These agent cards define each agents capabilities and endpoints. The remote agent performs a task autonomously and returns data or results without access to the client’s internal context — an essential feature for enterprise deployments, as it respects autonomy and privacy boundaries. Figure 2: A2A Protocol Communication Architecture
A2A’s structured messaging and modular architecture deliver five notable benefits for enterprise-wide coordination:
Interoperability at scale: Agents from different environments interact through a shared, vendor-neutral standard. Security by design: OAuth-based authentication and encrypted transport layers ensure compliance and data protection. Real-time context flow: Server-Sent Events (SSE)-based streaming keeps agent interactions dynamic and state-aware. Modular task orchestration: Task lifecycles, whether submitted, processing, or complete, are easily tracked for transparency and monitoring. Ecosystem resilience: JSON-RPC (JavaScript Object Notation Remote Procedure Call) versioning enables backward compatibility as new capabilities emerge. By using the A2A protocol, organizations can connect their entire AI ecosystem into one collaborative network. This allows agents to communicate, share goals, and synchronize operations. MCP vs A2A: Core Differences, Best Fit, and Strategic Choice
Enterprise IT leaders exploring different agentic AI architectures face a strategic decision: when does it make sense to use the Model Context Protocol (MCP), the Agent-to-Agent protocol (A2A), or both? The answer lies in understanding their complementary roles and deployment scenarios.
MCP serves as a universal adapter, connecting AI agents to tools, APIs, and data sources, while A2A is the standard for secure, structured communication and delegation between autonomous AI agents. Each protocol effectively addresses a different layer of interoperability: MCP standardizes access to capabilities (how agents interact with the outside world), while A2A enables collaborative workflows (how AI agents work together). For enterprises, the decision is less about the merits of one protocol versus the other than about the appropriate protocol that supports the desired outcome: streamlined data/tool connectivity, scalable multi-agent orchestration, or both. Most modern, scalable agentic AI systems will ultimately leverage both protocols for full-stack collaboration (MCP for reliable tool and context integration, and A2A for orchestrating teamwork across agents and distributed processes).

Organizations considering implementing multi-agent collaboration platforms must strategically align protocol selection with their objectives. The Model Context Protocol (MCP) and Agent-to-Agent Protocol (A2A) serve complementary yet unique purposes, addressing different levels of enterprise AI orchestration. Here are a few strategic considerations for protocol selection and integration:
MCP stands out for providing granular, secure, and flexible connectivity between AI agents and a wide variety of enterprise data sources, Application Programming Interfaces (APIs), and tools. It establishes a standardized interface facilitating context preservation, long-running agent workflows, and seamless tool invocation. Organizations that value context-aware AI models capable of integrating with proprietary systems, managing state, and extending toolsets will find MCP an essential protocol.
In contrast, A2A focuses on the inter-agent communication, task delegation, and collaborative orchestration elements needed for distributed multi-agent workflows that require more complex coordination. Its architecture allows for the discovery, authentication, and coordination of autonomous AI agents across decentralized platforms and business domains. Enterprises that wish to tap into cross-functional automation, multi-domain collaboration, and resilient process orchestration will find A2A useful. The best enterprise AI strategies often involve a combination of both protocols to capitalize on the full potential of the multi-agent systems. MCPs context and robust tooling provide the foundational capabilities for individual agents, while A2A allows these enriched agents to collaborate in a secure, scalable, and governed environment. Therefore, organizations that invest in a layered protocol architecture position themselves to maximize operational performance, agility, and innovation.
Implementation and Governance Considerations
Deploying MCP and A2A protocols successfully demands a balance between governance, infrastructure, and organizational readiness.
Strengthening the Technical Foundation
Organizations should begin with a clear interoperability architecture. The MCP implementations rely on API gateways, context-sharing security layers, and strong data permissions. On the other hand, the A2A-enabled systems require agent registries, messaging infrastructure, and standardized identity management. Aligning both with cloud or hybrid architectures ensures AI agents can scale efficiently without compromising on control.
Embedding Governance from the Start
Security & governance for multi-agent systems must extend beyond compliance. A Deloitte survey found that trust is one of the main challenges in industries such as finance and accounting. When asked about AI agents autonomy, 59.7% of respondents trust them to make decisions only within a defined framework, while humans should handle judgment calls. Only 2.7% fully trust AI to make all decisions, and 19.9% do not trust AI in any decision-making. [1]
It’s imperative for leaders to create cross-functional committees from IT, data, and legal to define agent lifecycles. Establish clear rules when it comes to agent autonomy, data handling, and escalation protocols, especially when decisions impact regulated processes. Ongoing monitoring and audit trails are essential to ensure trust, transparency, and accountability as agents act autonomously. Managing Change and Accountability
Human teams need to understand how and why AI agents work. Transparent communication, training of adaptable skills, and engaging stakeholders build confidence in autonomous systems and facilitate overall acceptance. Begin with measurable pilot deployments that demonstrate safe, explainable agent behavior, then expand gradually. Find a balance between “ambitious” automation and governance maturity.
The Future of Enterprise Intelligence: Powered by Interoperability
Multi-agent collaboration will enter its operational phase in 2026. According to Forrester, 75% of CX leaders now view AI as a human amplifier rather than a replacement, and 61% of organizations believe that agentic AI has transformative potential. The value of robust, multi-agent collaboration and agentic AI-centric protocol standardization is well understood. With high interoperability, organizations are unlocking the agility and better performance of multi-agent AI systems. Recently, Accenture found that companies with highly interoperable applications grew revenues approximately six times faster than their non-interoperable peers, while also capturing more than 5 points of incremental annual growth compared to competitors. Amidst the challenges posed by data silos and fragmented architectures to next-generation enterprise intelligence, MCP and A2A protocols provide the groundwork for unified, context-rich, and adaptive Agentic AI ecosystems. For enterprise IT leaders, the road ahead is abundantly clear: focus on interoperability as a base-level priority; align protocol decisions to strategic goals; and embrace multi-agent collaboration.

Developers have long relied on RESTful APIs as the glue between applications. But as AI systems and language models grow more capable and need to interact with a sprawling landscape of tools and data, the old REST paradigm is starting to show its age. Enter Model Context Protocol (MCP) — a new open standard that promises to streamline integration, reduce friction, and unlock richer capabilities for AI-driven applications. This post explores why you should consider transitioning from traditional RESTful APIs to MCP, highlighting the pain points of the status quo and how MCP resolves them. We’ll compare the experience of manually wiring up function calls versus adopting MCP’s standardized approach, weigh the pros and cons, and discuss how using an MCP gateway can make the transition far easier. Along the way, we’ll look at real examples (like the projects Unla and Peta) that showcase the benefits of making the switch.
The Limitations of RESTful APIs in an AI-Driven World
RESTful APIs have been a staple of software development for good reason — they are language-agnostic, leverage HTTP, and have well-understood patterns. However, when integrating AI agents or assistants with dozens of services, the REST approach can become a bottleneck. Each new integration often means writing a custom connector or wrapper for a specific API, teaching the AI how to call it, handle auth, parse responses, and so on. Over time, these one-off integrations pile up into a fragile web of custom code.
One major challenge is the explosive integration complexity that arises when scaling AI across many tools. If you have M different AI clients or models and N different services to connect to, a naïve approach might require up to M×N bespoke integrations — an untenable “integration explosion” . In an enterprise setting, this could mean hundreds of custom connectors, which is costly to build and maintain and prone to breaking as APIs change . As a Neo4j blog put it, without a shared standard like MCP, developers end up “stitching together ad-hoc APIs, mixing SDKs that don’t align, and maintaining fragile interfaces that models can’t reliably use.” In other words, every new tool feels like a new project — hardly the agility we want when deploying AI solutions.
Inconsistency and lack of discoverability are additional pain points. Each REST API has its own endpoints, data formats, auth mechanisms, and idiosyncrasies. An AI agent must be explicitly taught or coded to use each one. There’s no universal way for a model to say “what actions can I perform?” or to seamlessly chain outputs from one API into inputs of another. Complex workflows — say, retrieving data from a database, then using it to call a SaaS service, then updating an internal system — require painstakingly orchestrating multiple HTTP calls and juggling intermediate state on the client side. REST APIs by themselves are stateless, so maintaining context across multiple calls is a developer’s responsibility. This makes it difficult for AI-driven applications to perform multi-step reasoning or actions without a lot of custom glue code. In short, traditional REST integrations can be rigid and labor-intensive, which stifles the dynamic, adaptive potential of AI.
Security is another growing concern. To let an AI assistant use a REST API, developers often have to embed API keys or credentials in the code or prompt. This raises the risk of sensitive keys leaking (for example, if an LLM inadvertently outputs them). Additionally, once an AI has access to an API, it may be hard to enforce fine-grained controls via REST alone — either the agent has the token and full access, or it doesn’t. Wrangling OAuth flows or ensuring an AI only performs allowed actions becomes yet another custom challenge for each integration.
Finally, scalability and monitoring issues emerge as the number of integrations grows. Without a unified approach, developers must instrument and monitor each API call individually, implement retries, rate limiting, and logging in disparate places. When something goes wrong in a complex chain of calls, tracing the issue across multiple services can be difficult. The lack of a central integration layer means inconsistent tools for auditing or controlling the AI’s tool usage.
These pain points have been tolerable at small scale or in simple use-cases. But as soon as you try to build a robust AI agent that taps into many systems, the shortcomings of manual REST integrations become clear. This is where the Model Context Protocol (MCP) comes into play — addressing these limitations head-on.
What is MCP and Why Does It Matter?
Model Context Protocol (MCP) is an open-source standard (originally introduced by Anthropic in late 2024) that provides a universal method for connecting AI applications to external systems . In essence, MCP acts like a “USB-C port” for AI — a single, standardized interface through which an AI agent can plug into any number of tools, databases, services, or workflows . Just as USB-C replaced a tangle of device-specific cables with one universal connector, MCP aims to replace ad-hoc integrations with one protocol that any AI client and any service can speak.
At a high level, MCP defines a simple client-server architecture for AI-tool interactions. An AI application (the “host”) connects to one or more MCP servers — each server exposing a set of capabilities (like functions it can perform or data it can provide) in a standardized format. An MCP client library handles the details of discovery and communication, so the AI can ask “what can you do?” and call those functions with the proper parameters and context . Under the hood, the protocol ensures every tool invocation and data exchange is done in a structured way that the AI model can understand and reliably incorporate into its reasoning.
The key here is standardization. Instead of every API having a unique contract and integration method, MCP provides a consistent wrapper for any action or data. For example, whether the underlying task is querying a SQL database, searching a document, or sending an email, to the AI it just looks like calling an MCP tool with a defined name and input/output schema. This consistency slashes development overhead because you no longer have to write one-off code for each service . As the official docs note, MCP was created specifically so that developers “don’t have to rebuild one-off integrations every time [they] connect an LLM to a new service.”
Crucially, MCP directly tackles the integration explosion problem. Rather than building M×N custom bridges, a tool provider can implement MCP once, and any AI client that supports MCP can use it — and vice versa . This one-to-many model mirrors the success of earlier web standards: just like embracing HTTP and REST enabled an explosion of interoperable web services, adopting MCP allows any AI to talk to any tool that follows the protocol . In fact, we’re already seeing the network effects. In MCP’s first year, thousands of public MCP servers have appeared (from dev tools to Fortune 500 backends), and major AI platforms like ChatGPT, Google’s Gemini, Microsoft Copilot, VS Code, and many others have added MCP support . In March 2025, OpenAI officially adopted MCP for its models, and Microsoft invested in the standard — clear signs that industry leaders see MCP as the future of AI integration . With cloud providers (AWS, GCP, Azure, Cloudflare, etc.) also offering infrastructure for MCP, the ecosystem is growing rapidly .
So why does MCP matter so much for developers? In short, it reduces the time and complexity involved in connecting AI capabilities to real-world systems . Instead of treating each new integration as a bespoke project, you plug into a ready-made ecosystem. Developers can focus on what the AI should do with the data or tool, rather than how to call each API. Early adopters report that this unlocks more ambitious workflows. For example, one user described how an AI agent could autonomously perform a multi-step process — fetching an ID from a Postgres database, using it to query Salesforce for details, then posting a summary to Slack — all through natural language instructions without any custom-coded integration logic . Such a seamless end-to-end workflow would be a “wow” moment for anyone who’s struggled to tie together three different REST APIs and business logic by hand.
Moreover, MCP was designed with robust context management and multi-step reasoning in mind. Unlike stateless REST calls, MCP interactions can be part of a session where the client (and by extension the AI) maintains context over multiple tool calls. This enables complex dialogues or operations that span multiple steps, all orchestrated by the AI agent. Instead of brittle sequential API calls wired together externally, the AI can dynamically decide which tools to use in what order, based on the conversation — a paradigm shift from static data retrieval to active reasoning and orchestration . In practical terms, this means an AI assistant can handle more sophisticated tasks, consulting various resources and taking actions much like a human agent would, but with the MCP layer ensuring each step is executed properly and securely.
Security and governance are also first-class considerations in MCP’s design. The protocol emphasizes explicit user approval and sandboxing of tools by default . An AI can only use tools that have been deliberately connected and authorized, preventing it from going rogue on the open internet. For self-hosted scenarios, MCP servers often run locally or in controlled environments unless explicitly exposed remotely, keeping sensitive data under your oversight . Additionally, because all interactions funnel through the MCP client/server interface, it’s easier to audit and apply policies uniformly. We’ll touch more on advanced security controls when we discuss MCP gateways like Peta, but it’s worth noting that moving to MCP can actually enhance security compared to ad-hoc scripts calling REST. By centralizing how tools are invoked, you gain a chokepoint to inject credentials securely, enforce role-based access, or require human approval for certain high-impact actions — things that are very hard to bolt on after the fact in a traditional integration.
In summary, MCP matters because it addresses the very problems that RESTful APIs present in the era of AI agents: it standardizes tool access, cuts down integration effort, enables richer interactions, and lays a foundation of scalability and security for the next generation of AI-enabled software.
Manual Function Calls vs. Adopting MCP — A Developer’s Perspective
How does building AI integrations with MCP actually differ from the traditional approach? Let’s compare the experiences:
Manual REST API Integration (Status Quo):
Pros:
Fine-Grained Control: You’re calling each API directly, so you can handle every request and response exactly as needed. There are no new abstractions to learn — it’s plain HTTP requests, which every web developer understands.
Simplicity for Single Use-Cases: For a very small number of integrations (say your chatbot only ever needs one internal API), writing a targeted script or using OpenAI’s function calling for that API might be straightforward. You avoid introducing another layer (no additional infrastructure beyond the API itself).
Maturity and Tools: REST has been around for decades, so there are countless debugging tools, logging systems, and best practices. Developers likely already have pipelines and monitoring set up for their APIs.
Cons:
Heavy Development Overhead: Each new function the AI needs to perform often requires writing new code or prompts. For example, if you want your AI assistant to fetch customer info, update an order, and send an email, that might involve three separate API integrations coded manually. This doesn’t scale — building “countless custom integrations” quickly becomes costly and unsustainable as use cases expand .
Fragmentation: Every API has its own auth and data format. You end up dealing with API keys, OAuth tokens, JSON payload structures, etc., on a case-by-case basis. The logic for calling each service is siloed, which makes it hard to reuse or generalize. There’s no common schema or discovery mechanism to leverage.
Maintenance Burden: Because these integrations are essentially brittle one-offs, any change — an API version update, a new required parameter, etc. — means you must manually update your code/prompt. It’s easy for things to break. When you have dozens of such functions, maintenance becomes a significant ongoing task.
Limited AI Autonomy: The AI can only do exactly what you’ve hard-coded or anticipated. If a user’s request doesn’t map neatly onto the predefined actions, the system either fails or requires a human developer to add a new capability. This fixed action space limits the AI’s flexibility and usefulness.
Orchestration Complexity: Handling multi-step workflows or conditional logic with manual calls is complex. The developer has to implement the sequence and control flow, or use an agent framework that itself requires a lot of setup. The AI isn’t truly “choosing” its actions freely; it’s following a script or at best selecting from predefined options.
Using the Model Context Protocol:
Pros:
Standardized Integration: With MCP, the way the AI calls a database versus a SaaS API versus a local tool is the same. The AI doesn’t need custom coding for each — it discovers available actions through the protocol. This dramatically lowers the effort to add a new tool or data source; often it’s a matter of configuration rather than code . Developers avoid writing repetitive boilerplate, speeding up development.
Dynamic Discovery: An MCP-compliant AI client can query an MCP server to list its capabilities and expected inputs/outputs . This means the AI’s action space can be flexible and extensible. If tomorrow you connect a new service via MCP, the AI can immediately see and use it. We’re no longer constrained to what was built in at launch.
Unified Context & Chaining: Because MCP calls are handled through a common client, the AI can more naturally chain operations and carry context between them. The MCP client manages session state, so an AI agent can perform multi-step reasoning (e.g. use output of tool A as input to tool B) within one conversation/session. The developer doesn’t have to manually funnel data from one API to the next — the AI orchestrates it through the MCP layer.
Reduced Cognitive Load for AI: Perhaps surprisingly, using MCP can make it easier for the AI model itself to function correctly. As one commentator noted, without a unifying standard, an agent would have to “know every app’s API and write the right function call code for each one — which is a huge ask for any LLM” . In other words, expecting a language model to memorize or be trained on countless unique API formats is unrealistic. MCP standardizes everything, so the model only has to learn one way of calling functions, and it can interact with any app that speaks MCP . This leads to more reliable and consistent outcomes, since the format of tool calls is predictable for the model.
Interoperability and Ecosystem: Tools integrated via MCP are immediately available to a wide range of AI clients (ChatGPT, Claude, IDE plugins, etc.), not just your specific application . Likewise, your AI agent can leverage the growing catalog of MCP-enabled tools and connectors out-of-the-box. You get to stand on the shoulders of community contributions — everything from Google Calendar connectors to code execution sandboxes might be plug-and-play. This “build once, use anywhere” benefit is something REST on its own never achieved (since each API is an island).
Built-in Governance: MCP’s structure allows for centralized governance of tool usage. Because calls funnel through an MCP client/server, it’s easier to implement logging, rate limiting, or access control in one place. You can attach policies (like “the AI cannot delete records, only read or create”) at the MCP server level, rather than trusting the AI to follow guidelines in prompt. As we’ll discuss with MCP gateways, you can even enforce human approval for certain actions. This central management of AI actions is a game-changer for safe deployment in production environments.
Cons:
Learning Curve: MCP is a new technology, and it introduces its own concepts (hosts, clients, servers, tool manifests, etc.). Developers will need to get familiar with the MCP specification and possibly new frameworks or libraries. There may be some setup involved in running MCP servers or gateways, which is new territory if you’re only used to calling HTTP endpoints. The good news is the community is growing fast, with official SDKs in all major languages and extensive documentation, but there is still an adoption curve.
Evolving Standard: As of 2025, MCP is still maturing. The spec has periodic releases and improvements (e.g. recent additions for async operations and stateless calls) . Early adopters might face breaking changes or need to update their implementations as MCP evolves. That said, its core is stabilizing, and the backing by the Linux Foundation’s Agentic AI Foundation signals long-term support and stability . It’s a trade-off between getting benefits now vs. dealing with some “growing pains” of a young standard.
Infrastructure Overhead: In a basic REST integration, you call an API directly. With MCP, you often introduce an MCP server or gateway in between. This extra layer can add a bit of latency (usually minimal) and complexity in deployment. You’ll need to host/configure that MCP layer somewhere. However, many solutions (like lightweight gateways or cloud-managed MCP services) make this pretty painless, and the advantages in capability usually outweigh the slight overhead.
Requires Tool Support: To fully leverage MCP, the services or APIs you want to use ideally have MCP interfaces (or you provide them via a gateway). If a particular third-party API isn’t MCP-enabled yet, you might have to implement a wrapper or wait for the ecosystem to catch up. In practice, this is similar to how not every service had an API initially — there may be some lag before everything you want is available as MCP. The community is quickly wrapping common services, and tools like Unla can wrap any REST API on the fly (more on that next), so this gap is closing rapidly.
Debugging Mindset Shift: When an AI is autonomously calling tools via MCP, debugging can involve looking at the interaction logs between the AI and the MCP server, rather than step-by-step imperative code. Developers might need to use new monitoring tools (e.g. MCP inspector or gateway UIs) to see what the agent is doing. While this is just a different way of working, it can feel less straightforward at first compared to logging a sequence of HTTP requests in code.
Overall, the pros of MCP tend to far outweigh the cons when you’re aiming to build complex, scalable AI integrations. The upfront effort to learn and set up MCP is quickly repaid by not having to write boilerplate for every new tool or troubleshoot myriad custom pipelines. As AI applications move toward more agentic behavior — where we want models that can autonomously decide how to use tools — having a standard like MCP is almost a prerequisite. It provides the foundation for safe, manageable autonomy, whereas the manual approach would crumble under the weight of so many bespoke parts.
Smooth Transition via MCP Gateways
You might be thinking, “This sounds great in theory, but we already have a bunch of REST APIs — do we have to rewrite everything to use MCP?” Thankfully, no. One of the most practical ways to adopt MCP is by using an MCP gateway as a bridge between your existing APIs and the new protocol. MCP gateways are intermediary services or proxies that sit between an AI (the MCP client/host) and your back-end APIs or databases (which may not natively speak MCP). The gateway translates standardized MCP calls from the AI into the appropriate REST/SQL/other calls to your system, and then returns the results in a way the AI understands. In effect, it lets you wrap all your existing services behind a single MCP-compatible interface without altering those services.
Many MCP gateway solutions have emerged, ranging from open-source projects to commercial platforms . These gateways often come with useful features out of the box: authentication handling, scaling and load balancing, auditing and logging of AI tool usage, rate limiting, and UIs for configuration and monitoring . By providing a management layer, they make it feasible to deploy AI agents in production where you need reliability and oversight on top of raw functionality .
Perhaps the best part is how easily you can get started. Some gateways allow you to expose a legacy REST API as an MCP-compatible tool with minimal effort. For instance, ContextForge (an open-source MCP gateway backed by IBM) can aggregate multiple REST/gRPC services and present them as a single MCP endpoint for your AI. It effectively virtualizes legacy APIs as MCP tools, enabling an LLM agent to use those APIs without any custom integration code . That means you could plug in internal microservices or third-party APIs you already rely on, and the AI will see them as just more tools in its toolbox.
To make this concrete, let’s look at two prominent projects — Unla and Peta — which exemplify the range of options for MCP gateways and the benefits they bring.
Unla: Wrapping REST APIs into MCP in Minutes
[ ] Unla is a popular open-source MCP gateway known for its simplicity and lightweight approach. Its creators describe it as a way to “instantly transform your existing APIs or services into MCP endpoints without writing any code.” Under the hood, Unla is essentially a configurable proxy (written in Go) that you can deploy alongside your services. You provide a YAML configuration describing your API’s endpoints and their inputs/outputs, and Unla will expose those as if they were tools on an MCP server . This means if you have, say, a trusty internal HTTP service (or even a GraphQL or gRPC service) that isn’t MCP-aware, you don’t need to rewrite it — you can wrap it with Unla and immediately make it accessible to AI agents via standardized MCP calls .
What makes Unla especially attractive is how low-effort it is. The project offers a one-command Docker launch that brings up the Unla gateway plus a web-based management UI . Through this UI, you can live-configure tools: add a new endpoint, define its parameters, and test it out by chatting with it — all through a friendly interface. No complex deployment or code changes needed; it’s very much a “plug-and-play” solution for enabling MCP. Many developers have used Unla to quickly connect AI agents to their existing services, which is great for hackathons, prototypes, or augmenting a product without a huge refactor . For example, if you have a legacy CRM with a REST API, you can write a short Unla config mapping the CRM’s HTTP endpoints to MCP tool functions, and in minutes your AI assistant (be it ChatGPT or another MCP-enabled model) can start pulling customer data from that CRM on demand . This would have been a multi-day integration effort in the old world; with Unla it becomes almost trivial.
The no-code integration aspect of Unla is a big win for productivity. As noted in a review, you simply declare your API interface in YAML and “Unla does the rest”, which “dramatically lowers the effort to integrate an AI with new systems.” . This also opens the door for non-developers or small teams to get involved — for instance, a solutions engineer could configure an MCP tool without writing Python/Java code, expanding who can contribute to AI enablement. Unla is also quite efficient (being written in Go) and can be scaled behind load balancers or in clusters for higher availability . It’s a zero-intrusion layer — you don’t have to modify your existing APIs at all, which is a relief when dealing with delicate legacy systems .
In short, Unla exemplifies the ease of transitioning to MCP. It shows that you can start taking advantage of MCP immediately, using configuration instead of coding, and without ripping out or changing your current services. This lowers the barrier to entry significantly. You get many of MCP’s benefits — standardized AI access, quick tool onboarding, central management — with minimal risk and time investment. Unla’s popularity (evident from its thousands of GitHub stars and active community) attests to how empowering this approach has been for developers looking to modernize their stack for AI .
Peta: Enterprise-Grade MCP Gateway with Security in Mind
On the other end of the spectrum is Peta, a commercial MCP gateway solution that focuses on delivering enterprise-level security, compliance, and control. If Unla is about quick enablement, Peta is about safe and controlled enablement at scale. The product markets itself as “1Password for AI Agents”, which is a hint at its emphasis on secrets management and zero-trust principles .
In an AI integration context, one big concern is how to prevent an AI from accidentally or maliciously exposing sensitive credentials or performing unauthorized actions. Peta tackles this by combining a secure credential vault, a zero-trust MCP proxy, and a human-in-the-loop approval system in one platform . Concretely, with Peta, you don’t give raw API keys to the AI. Instead, secrets (API tokens, database passwords, etc.) are stored encrypted in Peta’s vault, and the AI agent authenticates to Peta with a short-lived token or identity. When the AI tries to call an MCP tool (say, an internal payment processing API), Peta will inject the necessary credentials into the request on the server side, just for that single call, and strip them out of any response . The AI never sees the actual secret — so even if the conversation log were leaked, your keys remain safe . This design ensures that credentials are never exposed to the AI or anywhere outside the vault.
Furthermore, every tool invocation is mediated by Peta’s policy engine. You can define fine-grained access control rules and approval workflows in the Peta Console (a web admin interface) . For example, you might configure that the SalesAI agent is allowed to read from the customer database but not delete, or that any request to initiate a wire transfer must be approved by a human manager before execution. When the AI attempts those actions via MCP, Peta will check its identity, the requested action, and the policies: if something is outside the allowed scope, it can block or require a manual review before letting it through . Peta essentially acts as a gatekeeper for AI tool usage, giving organizations confidence that an autonomous agent won’t go rogue or violate compliance rules.
Peta is built to integrate into enterprise environments — it can tie into identity providers for auth, generate audit logs for every action, and even manage scaling of underlying MCP servers (spinning up more instances, doing health checks, etc.) to ensure reliability . Its use cases are all about critical systems: if you want an AI co-pilot to have access to production databases, financial systems, or sensitive internal APIs, Peta provides the safeguards to do so safely . Companies that must adhere to strict security standards (finance, healthcare, etc.) can use Peta to harness AI agents without compromising on oversight.
While Peta is a commercial product (with the support and polish that implies), it’s worth noting it doesn’t lock you into a proprietary system — it implements the MCP standard just with added layers on top. You could start with open-source MCP servers and later slot Peta in front of them for security, without having to rewrite your core logic . This highlights another benefit of MCP’s design: interoperability and choice. You can mix and match components (open-source or paid) as needed. For instance, use Unla or custom code for some tools and Peta for others that require strict control, all under the same overarching protocol that your AI understands.
Together, Unla and Peta show the versatility of MCP gateways. Unla demonstrates quick adoption and developer-friendly integration, while Peta demonstrates that enterprise-grade requirements can be met. Depending on your needs, you can choose a lightweight approach or a full-featured platform — either way, you’re leveraging MCP under the hood. The takeaway is that migrating from REST to MCP doesn’t mean starting from scratch. With gateways, you can incrementally transition, wrapping existing APIs one by one or as needed, all while continuing to support your current REST consumers. This hybrid approach lets you bring AI on board via MCP without disrupting other clients of your APIs.
Embracing the Future: From REST to MCP
The evolution from RESTful APIs to the Model Context Protocol feels reminiscent of past shifts in technology. We went from proprietary data silos to SQL and REST as universal access patterns; now we’re moving from isolated AI integrations to a universal AI-to-tool interface. MCP is not about throwing away REST — it’s about building on top of it with a layer tailored for AI. In fact, many MCP servers will internally use REST or database queries or other protocols to fulfill the AI’s requests. What changes is the external contract: instead of a patchwork of endpoints and formats, we present a consistent, machine-discoverable interface that smart agents can work with fluidly.
For developers, the promise of MCP is to save time, reduce headaches, and enable capabilities that were previously out of reach. No more writing glue code for each new feature an AI assistant needs; no more worrying that an API change will break half your prompts; no more saying “sorry, our chatbot can’t do that” because it wasn’t in the spec. By adopting MCP (and using gateways where appropriate), you make your architecture more flexible and future-proof. Adding a new integration becomes as simple as plugging in a new MCP connector, which could be a trivial config file (thanks to tools like Unla) or an available module from the community. It shifts effort from repetitive coding to higher-level design: deciding what your AI should do rather than how to technically make it happen.
We’ve also seen that MCP can make AI deployments more robust and governable, which is critical as we trust these systems with more responsibility. Standardization naturally brings better tooling — from monitoring dashboards to debugging utilities — because those tools can cater to the single MCP interface instead of countless bespoke ones. And when it comes to safety, solutions like Peta illustrate that you can have fine-grained control and transparency over AI actions. It’s a lot easier to secure one unified pipeline of actions than a tangle of separate API calls that might slip under the radar.
Is MCP a silver bullet for all integration woes? Of course not — no abstraction is free of trade-offs. But in the balance, MCP addresses a clear need in the AI developer community. It takes the hard-learned lessons of past integration frameworks and applies them to the fast-moving world of AI. The fact that major tech companies and open-source communities are rallying around it is a strong signal. Even in its youth, MCP has demonstrated value by simplifying real-world projects and enabling things that were impractical before.
In practical terms, making the switch can be gradual. You might start by deploying an MCP gateway in front of a couple of your APIs and allowing your AI agent to use them, while everything else remains unchanged. Over time, as confidence grows, more tools can be brought into the fold. If you’re building a new system from scratch, you might go MCP-first, exposing an MCP server alongside (or instead of) a traditional API. And if you’re an AI tooling or platform developer, making your product MCP-compatible can instantly broaden its reach, as any MCP-speaking AI can integrate with it easily.
In conclusion, moving from RESTful APIs to Model Context Protocol is about unlocking efficiency and capability. It’s about giving AI the standardized bridge it needs to seamlessly interact with the rich world of software and data we’ve built with REST. Developers should consider this transition not as a rip-and-replace of existing tech, but as an upgrade — akin to adding a powerful new engine to your application while keeping the wheels that already work. The pain points of manual integration are real, and MCP offers a compelling remedy. By embracing MCP (with the help of gateways like Unla for quick wins and Peta for secure scale), you position yourself at the forefront of the next wave in software development, where AI isn’t a black-box oracle on the side, but an integrated, context-aware participant in our systems. The tools and community support are ready — and after all, if you could save yourself hundreds of hours of integration drudgery while opening up new possibilities for intelligent features, why stick with the old way? It’s time to plug into the future with MCP.
