Can We Use Both MCP and A2A?
Practically, many enterprises use both protocols together. MCP ensures each agent has the right context and tools, while A2A enables those agents to collaborate effectively across complex workflows. This combination maximizes efficiency, scalability, and security.
Choosing the right protocol or layering both is a strategic decision. By understanding the strengths of MCP and A2A, enterprises can design AI ecosystems that are not only powerful but cohesive, context-aware, and collaborative.
Misconceptions Related To MCP and A2A
Despite their power, MCP and A2A protocol are often misunderstood. A few common misconceptions include:
MCP is only for complex systems: Many assume MCP is useful only in large-scale setups, but it also simplifies single-agent workflows by standardizing tool access and task execution.
A2A is just messaging between agents: While A2A enables agent communication, it is more than a messaging layer- it orchestrates task lifecycles, artifact exchange, and user interface negotiation.
Agents must be human-like: Some think agents need human-like reasoning to use MCP or A2A effectively. In reality, these protocols focus on structured coordination, tool usage, and reliable task handling, independent of human-like intelligence.
Security and governance are optional: Another misconception is that cross-agent protocols compromise safety. Both MCP and A2A are designed with access control, authentication, and observability in mind.
MCP and A2A are mutually exclusive: Users may believe you have to choose one protocol over the other. In practice, they complement each other- MCP strengthens single-agent capabilities, while A2A enables multi-agent orchestration.

Final Thoughts
As enterprises scale AI, protocols like MCP and A2A are no longer optional; they are essential. MCP ensures agents have the right context and tools to operate efficiently, while A2A enables seamless collaboration between multiple agents across workflows and platforms. Together, they create a powerful, interoperable AI ecosystem capable of handling complex tasks, automating processes, and driving productivity. Choosing the right protocol or combining both strategically can make the difference between fragmented, siloed AI and a cohesive, high-performing agent network. For Enterprises aiming to lead in the AI era, understanding and adopting these protocols is the first step toward future-ready, scalable intelligence.

Frequently Asked Questions
Can MCP replace A2A?
While both standards improve AI interoperability, MCP cannot fully replace A2A because they solve different architectural challenges. MCP is designed to connect a single agent to tools and data, whereas A2A focuses on coordinating communication and task handoffs between multiple independent agents. Using them together creates a more scalable AI ecosystem.
What is the difference between A2A vs MCP?
The primary difference between MCP and A2A lies in their functional scope and architecture. MCP uses a client-server model to provide agents with external context and tool access, while A2A utilizes a peer-to-peer model for agent collaboration. While MCP anchors an agent in data, A2A enables agents to negotiate and share tasks across different systems.
Can MCP and A2A be used together?
Yes, combining MCP and A2A is often the ideal strategy for enterprise agentic workflows. In this hybrid setup, MCP ensures each individual agent has standardized access to the tools it needs, while A2A manages the high-level orchestration and communication between those agents. This layering maximizes both internal agent intelligence and external collaborative efficiency.
What is MCP and A2A in agentic AI?
MCP and A2A serve as the critical communication backbone. MCP acts as the universal connector for models to interact with databases and APIs, while A2A provides the common language for agents to work together on complex goals. Is A2A part of MCP?

They serve complementary purposes: MCP enhances individual agent capabilities, and A2A orchestrates multi-agent workflows for collaboration and shared task completion.
What is one limitation of MCP that A2A addresses?

Introduction
The Agent-to-Agent (A2A) Protocol is an open standard designed to enable autonomous AI agents to communicate, collaborate, and coordinate across different systems. It was introduced by Google DeepMind in early 2024 to support scalable, multi-agent ecosystems. A2A uses a structured message format that allows agents to negotiate tasks, share tools, and delegate responsibilities securely and efficiently. By promoting interoperability, it lays the groundwork for complex, modular AI workflows across diverse platforms.
To ground these concepts, let’s walk through how I built a multi-agent research assistant — essentially an AI system that autonomously fetches the latest research papers on a topic, summarizes and analyzes them, and presents results to the user. This project serves as a proof-of-concept for an A2A-style architecture. In this article I’ll focus on the high-level design and how the agents interact, rather than the low-level code (all implementation details are available in the linked repo at the end).
If you want to take a deeper dive into A2A altegother here is an article I wrote talking about A2A more broadly.
Overview of the Application
Goal: The research assistant automates an academic literature review for a given topic. A user provides a topic (e.g. “AI safety” or “quantum computing”) and some parameters like a date range. The system will then:
Fetch recent papers related to that topic.
Summarize each paper (producing a concise abstract).
Critique/Score each paper on certain dimensions (novelty, relevance, etc.).
Analyze Trends across the papers (find emerging topics).
Plan a Reading List of the top papers and generate a summary report for the user.
This pipeline naturally breaks down into different tasks — perfect for different agents to handle. I implemented the following agents (each as an independent component of the system):
Fetcher Agent: Searches external resources for new papers on the topic (in my example I query the arXiv API and Semantic Scholar API). It compiles a list of papers (title, authors, publication date, a PDF URL, and an ID like DOI or arXiv ID) and filters out any that were already seen in previous runs. The Fetcher then returns this list of paper metadata as its output, and also stores the metadata in a local database for persistence. This agent essentially acts as a bridge to external data sources — a good example of one agent using tools (HTTP APIs) and then passing the result to others.
Summarizer Agent: This agent takes each paper’s PDF (using the URL from the Fetcher) and produces a 5-line summary abstract of the paper and future improvement ideas. This is a heavy-lifting agent because it may need to download and read PDFs that are dozens of pages long. I built in a lot of robustness here. The Summarizer attempts to download the PDF and extract text; if the PDF is too large, it splits the text into chunks and uses an iterative summarization approach to condense it gradually. This handles the token overflow problem by chunking and “recursively summarizing” until the content fits within a prompt window. If the PDF download or parsing fails (which happens e.g. due to format issues or network errors), the Summarizer falls back to alternative strategies: it will try to fetch an official abstract from an API (arXiv or Semantic Scholar) in parallel with asking an LLM to generate a summary from just the title. Whichever returns first (the abstract or the LLM’s guess) is used as surrogate content, which it then summarizes with the same method. This ensures we don’t get stuck on a single paper — every paper yields at least some summary unless all methods fail. Additionally, the Summarizer agent asks the LLM to suggest 3–5 “future improvement ideas” or research directions based on the paper’s content. These ideas (possible follow-up work or unresolved questions from the paper) are saved to the database for later use, but are not part of the main output passed to the next agent (they’re more like a side artifact we wanted to capture for the user’s benefit).
Critic Agent: Reviews each paper’s summary and gives it three scores — for novelty, methodological soundness, and relevance to the chosen topic — each on a 0–10 scale, along with a short textual critique. The Critic essentially plays the role of a peer reviewer. Under the hood, it prompts an LLM with a fixed instruction to rate the summary on those criteria and output a JSON with the scores and a critique sentence. The agent then parses that JSON and attaches the scores and critique to each paper’s record. It also updates the database so that the paper entry now contains these scores and critique for persistence. The Critic agent thus transforms a list of paper summaries into a list of scored papers. Separating this from summarization, follows single-responsibility: if I want to change how scoring is done or add a new metric, I can just modify this agent independently.
Trend Analyzer Agent: Looks at the collection of papers (particularly their summaries and publication dates) and identifies emerging trends or clusters of research. This agent operates on the whole set rather than individual papers. It works by embedding each paper’s summary into a vector (using an embedding model) and clustering the vectors to find groups of related papers. Then, for each cluster, it computes if that topic is “trending” by comparing how many papers in that cluster appeared in the last week versus the previous week. It labels each cluster with some representative keywords (using a TF-IDF on the summaries) for interpretability. Finally, it picks the top 5 clusters with the greatest growth and saves these as “trends” in the database. For example, it might output that “Graph Neural Networks” is a cluster with 3 papers this week vs 1 last week (growth +200%), whereas other topics are stagnant. The Trend agent’s output isn’t directly needed by the next agent in the pipeline (I treat it as a side-effect that populates a trends table). In A2A terms, it’s like a remote agent that mostly does internal work and logs an artifact for the user, without returning a structured result to the caller (aside from a success flag). I still included it in the workflow so that by the end, trend data is ready for presentation.
Planner Agent: This is the final agent that takes the scored papers and produces a Reading Plan for the user. It selects the top few papers to prioritize and generates a nicely formatted summary of them. The Planner in this system implements a simple strategy: it computes an overall score for each paper and picks the top 5 papers from the last ~2 weeks. It then prompts an LLM to write a short introduction and an ordered list of those top papers as a suggested “reading queue”. Essentially, it asks the LLM to take the list of best papers (with their titles) and make a friendly recommendation blurb (e.g. “1. Paper Title — this paper explores XYZ…”). The output of Planner is a final plan text — a few paragraphs and bullet points of recommendations. The agent saves this plan to a database table and doesn’t pass anything downstream (since it’s the last step). In an A2A context, you can think of the Planner as producing the ultimate artifact that the user cares about.
All these agents run sequentially to complete one full pipeline. I orchestrated them using a lightweight framework (LangChain’s LangGraph library) that lets you define a directed acyclic graph of tasks. The flow was: Fetcher → Summarizer → Critic → Trend → Planner, where each takes the previous output (or shared state) and I defined edges accordingly. This could have been done with explicit A2A HTTP calls between independent services, but for simplicity I ran them in-process and in sequence (passing Python data structures). However, the design mirrors A2A: each agent class had a uniform run(input, state) -> (output, state) interface, akin to handling a task message and returning an artifact. This made it conceptually easy to swap implementations or even imagine each agent as a microservice.
Handling Long Tasks and Asynchronous Execution
One of the challenges was that the entire pipeline can take quite a while — especially if it fetches, say, 20 papers and has to summarize all of them (each requiring multiple LLM calls). Running this synchronously on a web request would be impractical (it could take minutes). This is where we applied A2A’s principle of supporting long-running tasks by integrating a background task queue.
I used Celery (a distributed task queue) to run the multi-agent pipeline in a worker process, separate from the user-facing interface. In practice, when a user kicks off a job (through the UI or API), the system enqueues a Celery task that will execute the Fetcher→…→Planner sequence in the background. This decoupling has several benefits aligned with A2A philosophy:
The user (or the client agent, in A2A terms) doesn’t have to hang waiting for the result. Instead, it can poll for status or be notified when done. I implemented a polling mechanism (the UI checks the job status every few seconds) similar to how one might use A2A’s polling or push notification approach to handle a long task asynchronously.
I can scale the worker horizontally. If multiple users start research jobs, Celery can handle them concurrently on multiple workers. Each worker still goes through the agent pipeline sequentially for a job, but different jobs don’t block each other. This mirrors an A2A scenario where multiple instances of an agent could handle tasks in parallel.
If the process crashes or needs to be retried, Celery can restart the task or mark it failed without breaking the frontend. I also implemented checkpointing in a sense — after each agent, results were written to the database. So even if something went wrong mid-pipeline, partial data (e.g., fetched papers) was not lost. This is analogous to an agent sending interim progress messages or artifacts in A2A.
A2A’s spec outlines that long tasks can be handled via status updates and final artifact delivery. In my case, the Celery worker writes log entries to a database table for each significant event (e.g., “Fetcher found 18 papers”, “Summarizer completed 17/18 papers, 1 skipped”) and marks the job as finished when done. The client side polls these logs to show a live progress feed to the user. This pattern is very much in the spirit of A2A (though we rolled our own solution): it provides real-time feedback during a lengthy operation, keeping the user informed.
State Persistence and Data Sharing
I chose to use a simple SQLite database as a shared state store for the agents. Each agent, as noted, writes its outputs to the DB: the Fetcher adds new records to a papers table, the Summarizer updates those records with summaries (and creates entries in a future_ideas table), the Critic updates scores in the papers table, Trend writes to a trends table, and Planner writes the final plan to a plans table. This persistent state serves multiple purposes:
Memory between agents: Because I didn’t implement in-memory agent-to-agent calls, the database ensured that even if the process was distributed, another agent could pick up the data. For example, the Critic doesn’t need to receive a Python list of papers from the Summarizer directly; it could query the papers table for all papers that have a summary but no scores yet. In this single-process pipeline I didn’t need to do that, but having the DB allowed flexibility (and indeed the Planner actually queries the DB for the top papers rather than relying on in-memory data passed, to ensure it has the latest scores).
Result snapshots: After a job finishes, I create a snapshot of the key results (reading plan, all trends, all papers with summaries and scores, all future ideas) in a separate results table as one JSON bundle. This is purely to make it quick to fetch everything the frontend needs in one go. The snapshot approach is handy for post-mortem analysis too — one can inspect old results without rerunning the pipeline. This is analogous to the final artifact in an A2A task lifecycle — I bundle all artifacts into one package. I even include the agent logs in the job record. This proved invaluable for debugging and for allowing the UI to display past results without recomputation.
Failure recovery: If something went wrong partway (say the LLM service was down during summarization), I could potentially restart the job and the Fetcher agent would know not to duplicate papers it already logged, etc., because the DB state is still there (I implemented an “idempotency” check so the fetcher skips papers already in the DB by ID). Having a persistent store means the agent system can be stateful across runs, which is important for continuous or iterative agents. (One could imagine an agent that continuously monitors new papers daily — it would rely on the stored state to know what’s new.)
The trade-off is that using a database introduces coupling (all agents share the DB schema). In a pure A2A architecture, you might instead have the client agent pass all needed data through messages to the next agent. I chose a DB for practicality and transparency — it was easier to inspect data and ensured nothing gets lost if a service restarts. In an enterprise A2A deployment, one might do similar or use an event store for agent communication. The key is that state persistence improved reliability, at the cost of some additional complexity.
Frontend Integration via Streamlit
I built a simple Streamlit web application as the user interface. An important design decision was to make the frontend communicate with the backend exclusively through REST API calls, never directly invoking the agents or database. This decoupling mirrors the idea that the UI (or a human user) could be considered another agent or client in the A2A ecosystem, interacting only via standardized interfaces.
The backend provides endpoints for: starting a new job, checking job status/logs, retrieving results, and clearing data. When the user enters a topic and hits “Run”, the Streamlit app does an HTTP POST to the backend’s /jobs endpoint with the parameters. The backend (a FastAPI app) then creates a job record and triggers the Celery task to run the pipeline. The response immediately returns a job ID (HTTP 202 Accepted) which the frontend uses to poll.
While the job is running, the frontend periodically GETs /jobs/<id> to fetch the latest status and logs. The backend API accumulates log lines from the database (or in-memory queue) and returns them as a text blob along with a status field (“queued”, “running”, “done”, or “failed”). The Streamlit app displays those logs in a text area so the user can see a live feed of what each agent is doing (e.g. “SummarizerAgent: processing paper 3/10…”). This is analogous to an A2A client using Server-Sent Events to get real-time updates — in our case we polled every few seconds which is simpler but conceptually similar.
Once the job status becomes “done”, the frontend makes a GET request to /jobs/<id>/result to fetch the final results package. The backend returns the JSON snapshot from the database (the reading plan, the trends list, papers list, etc.). The Streamlit app then renders these results for the user:
It shows the Suggested Reading Queue (the plan) as a formatted markdown section.
It shows Trending Topics with an expander for each cluster, listing the papers in that cluster. The user can click to toggle details for each paper — thanks to the stored data, we can display the paper’s summary, critique scores, and even a direct PDF link. This interactivity is all using the data that the agents produced.
It shows Future Improvement Ideas for each paper in a separate section, grouped by paper, so the user can read the brainstormed research directions.
Finally, it lists all papers in a table for reference.
All of these UI elements are constructed from the JSON result — no agent is called at view time. This means the frontend is entirely agnostic to how the data was produced; it only knows the schema of the result. I could even build a completely different UI (say a CLI tool or a chat interface) that hits the same endpoints and gets the same data. This separation of interface and implementation is a core benefit of the A2A style. The UI doesn’t need to embed an LLM or agent logic; it just requests a task (topic search) and later receives an artifact (the research summary package).
By interacting over REST, I also make it easier to later swap the Streamlit UI for something else, or let external applications call our research assistant as a service. In effect, I treated the whole pipeline as one composite agent that exposes a REST API (the client agent for the user), which internally coordinates with specialist agents (Fetcher, Summarizer, etc.). This is aligned with the A2A vision: you could expose an agent via an API and behind that single agent could be an army of sub-agents working together via A2A. The outside world doesn’t need to know the details.
Lessons Learned and Future Improvements
Building this multi-agent system taught me several lessons about applying A2A principles in practice:
Designing for Failure from the Start: In a multi-agent pipeline, you have to assume some part will eventually fail or produce unexpected output. I experienced failures like PDF downloads timing out, or the LLM returning too much text or malformed JSON. Our solution was to build fallback mechanisms at critical points (especially in the Summarizer). This significantly improved the robustness. The takeaway is: each agent should handle errors gracefully and communicate an actionable result whenever possible. If one agent can’t complete its task fully, maybe it returns a partial result or a flag that it skipped something, so the downstream agent or the orchestrator can decide what to do. A2A’s structured approach makes it easier to encode such flags (e.g., an agent could return an artifact with an “error” field). I used database entries and logs for this purpose. Future versions could make agents even more self-monitoring — e.g., the Critic could notice if a summary was missing and alert the orchestrator to re-run summarization for that paper.
Iterating and Adding Capabilities: The modular setup made it relatively easy to extend the system. For instance, the “Future Improvements” ideas generation was not in our initial prototype. I added it after the main pipeline was working, as an extra feature to provide more value to the user. Because it was conceptually a separate concern (brainstorming ideas for each paper), I had a choice: implement it as another agent or integrate it into an existing agent’s workflow. I chose to integrate into the Summarizer agent (to avoid an extra full pass over all papers), but isolated the logic in separate helper functions. This addition did not require changing the Critic, Trend, or Planner agents at all — those didn’t even need to know it exists. This experience underscores how new capabilities can be slotted in without upheaval. In an A2A architecture, I could just as well spawn a new “IdeasAgent” that subscribes to an event when a summary is created and outputs to a future_ideas artifact. The difference is mostly implementation detail. The key point is that modular agents and a shared communication standard mean the system is extensible.
Monitoring and Transparency: I found it extremely useful to log each agent’s actions and maintain results in a database for inspection. During development, this helped pinpoint where things went wrong (e.g., I could see that one paper’s summary was empty due to an edge-case in PDF parsing). For users, exposing the logs in real-time built trust — they could see exactly what the AI was doing (“why is it taking so long? oh, it’s summarizing a 30-page paper now.”). In a multi-agent world, transparency is vital; otherwise it can feel like a mysterious black box. I recommend designing your agents to produce meaningful logs or trace info and aggregating that for display. A2A doesn’t mandate how to do it, but the protocol’s philosophy of structured messages can be extended to structured logs or trace events.
Balancing Granularity of Agents: One design decision was how big or small to make each agent’s scope. Too fine-grained (e.g., a separate agent for downloading PDFs, another for splitting text, another for summarizing) would introduce a lot of overhead. Too coarse (one agent does everything from fetch to plan) defeats the purpose. I think my breakdown was effective, but there’s room to experiment. For example, one could merge Critic and Planner into a single “Analyzer Agent” that both scores and picks top papers (since those tasks are related). I kept them separate to allow possibly swapping out the scoring mechanism independently. This is a general lesson: decide agent boundaries based on independent deployability and expertise. If two tasks always need the same context and are simpler together, they might be one agent. If a task might be reused in other workflows (like “Critique a paper” could be useful standalone), it should be its own agent. A2A gives you the freedom to refactor these boundaries as you learn more, much like one refactors microservices.
Performance vs. Accuracy Trade-offs: In our pipeline, the slowest step was summarization (lots of LLM calls). I implemented parallelization for fallback (abstract vs LLM summary) using Python threads to save time, but we could do more — e.g., process multiple papers in parallel if we had the compute. An A2A architecture could naturally distribute such work: spawn multiple summarizer agents and assign papers to each. We didn’t go that far due to complexity, but it’s a next step. On accuracy, using GPT-4 for every step gave great results but is slow and costly; one could use smaller models or heuristics for some agents (e.g., a simpler model for initial filtering of papers). The A2A design lets you mix model sizes easily by agent. It also allows human-in-the-loop at agent boundaries: for instance, one could insert a human review after the Critic agent to validate scores. This wasn’t needed for our demo, but in a real use-case, the ability to inject human checks at defined points is a big advantage of a structured multi-agent pipeline.
Ecosystem and Standards: I manually orchestrated and integrated these agents, but going forward I expect frameworks to emerge that natively support A2A protocols. For example, if LangChain or other libraries fully support A2A messaging, I could have registered each agent and let a central router handle the calls via HTTP. My implementation was partially manual due to tool limitations at the time. I anticipate that in the near future, setting up an A2A system will become easier as standards solidify. In the meantime, I validated that even DIY approaches can yield a working system that adheres to A2A principles.
Conclusion
Google’s A2A protocol represents a significant step towards scalable, collaborative AI agents. By formalizing how agents communicate, A2A allows us to break complex problems into cooperating pieces — improving maintainability, testability, and reusability of AI components. In my multi-agent research assistant project, I saw these benefits firsthand: each agent had a clear role, which made the system easier to develop and extend, and the overall pipeline achieved something no single model could easily do alone.
Of course, designing multi-agent systems requires careful thought about architecture and infrastructure. There is added complexity in orchestrating asynchronous tasks, persisting state, and securing communications. However, the payoff is a more robust and modular system that can grow over time. Tasks that were once too big for one agent (or one prompt) become feasible when handled by an organized “team” of agents.
As A2A and similar standards gain adoption, I expect to see a flourishing ecosystem of specialized agents that can be composed like building blocks to create sophisticated AI-driven applications — from personal assistants that coordinate multiple services, to enterprise workflows that automate entire end-to-end processes. We’re essentially moving from single-agent intelligence toward multi-agent societies of AIs, each an expert in its niche, collectively more powerful than the sum of parts.
The journey is just beginning, and it’s an exciting time to experiment with these ideas. This research assistant project is open-sourced, so you can explore the implementation details and even run it yourself.

## 3. Core Concepts
144-
145-
- **Agent Discovery:** Clients find agents by fetching their `AgentCard` JSON, typically from a `/.well-known/agent-card.json` URI or a curated registry.
146-
- **Task Lifecycle:** Tasks progress through defined states (`submitted` -> `working` -> `completed`/`failed`, etc.), enabling tracking of long-running operations.
147-
- **Communication:** Interactions use `Message` objects containing `Part`s (text, file, data). Task outputs are delivered as `Artifact`s.
148-
- **Streaming:** Long-running tasks provide real-time updates via SSE using the `message/stream` method. Updates can be `Task`, `Message`, `TaskStatusUpdateEvent`, or `TaskArtifactUpdateEvent` objects.
149-
- **Push Notifications:** For disconnected clients, agents can send updates to a webhook URL configured via `CreateTaskPushNotificationConfig`.
150-
- **Authentication:** A2A leverages standard web security (e.g., OAuth, API keys), declared in the `AgentCard`. Credentials are sent via HTTP headers, not in the A2A payload.

153-
154-
- **Transport Security:** Production environments MUST use HTTPS with modern TLS.
155-
- **Authentication:** Servers MUST authenticate every request based on schemes declared in the `AgentCard`.
156-
- **Authorization:** Authorization logic is implementation-specific and MUST enforce the principle of least privilege, potentially on a per-skill basis.
157-
- **Push Notification Security:** Both the server (validating webhook URLs to prevent SSRF) and the client (verifying incoming notifications) have critical security responsibilities.
158-
- **Input Validation:** Servers MUST rigorously validate all RPC parameters and message content.

As artificial intelligence evolves from simple tools to sophisticated agents capable of complex reasoning and autonomous decision-making, the need for standardized communication becomes increasingly critical. Agents often need to collaborate to accomplish complex tasks that span multiple domains or require specialized capabilities. Without a common communication framework, integrating these diverse agents becomes a significant challenge, leading to brittle, custom solutions and hindering the development of scalable multi-agent systems.
Consider a travel planning scenario: A user wants to plan a week-long trip to Paris. This requires coordinating information and actions between multiple specialized agents handling flights, hotels, local activities, and ground transportation. Without a standardized protocol, each agent would need custom integration with every other agent involved, creating a complex and unmanageable web of incompatible interfaces.
Introducing the A2A Protocol
The Agent-to-Agent (A2A) Protocol addresses this challenge by establishing a standardized framework for communication between autonomous AI agents. Introduced by Google during its Google Cloud Next ’25 developer event in April 2025, A2A was developed in collaboration with over 50 technology partners and service providers, including major technology companies (Atlassian, Box, Cohere, Intuit, LangChain, MongoDB, PayPal, Salesforce, SAP, ServiceNow, UKG, Workday) and consulting partners (Accenture, BCG, Capgemini, Cognizant, Deloitte, HCLTech, Infosys, KPMG, McKinsey, PwC, TCS, Wipro).
A2A provides a common language and interaction pattern, enabling agents to communicate and collaborate effectively, regardless of their underlying implementation, provider, or specific function. It acts as a networking layer for the agentic AI ecosystem.

Core Principles
The A2A Protocol is built upon five fundamental principles that guide its design and ensure its effectiveness in enabling agent collaboration:
Embrace Agentic Capabilities: The protocol is designed for agents that possess autonomy and potentially complex reasoning abilities. It supports natural, potentially unstructured communication modalities, allowing agents to collaborate without sacrificing their specialized capabilities or requiring rigid, predefined interaction patterns.
Build on Existing Standards: A2A leverages well-established web technologies to ensure broad compatibility and ease of adoption. It utilizes HTTP for transport, Server-Sent Events (SSE) for real-time streaming, and JSON-RPC 2.0 for structured data exchange.
Secure by Default: Security is a primary consideration. A2A incorporates enterprise-grade authentication and authorization mechanisms, aligning with standard practices like OpenAPI security schemes, ensuring secure communication between agents.
Support for Long-Running Tasks: Agent interactions often involve tasks that take significant time to complete. A2A provides mechanisms for managing these long-running tasks, including status tracking, real-time feedback, state updates, and notifications.
Modality Agnostic: Communication between agents isn’t limited to text. A2A supports various modalities, including text, audio, video, and structured data, enabling rich multimedia interactions and accommodating diverse agent capabilities.
Architecture and Protocol Specification
A2A facilitates communication between a “client” agent initiating a request and a “remote” agent fulfilling it.
Transport Layer
A2A relies on standard web protocols:
HTTP/HTTPS: The primary transport protocol. Production implementations must use HTTPS with modern TLS ciphers for secure communication.
Server-Sent Events (SSE): Used for efficient, real-time, one-way streaming of updates (e.g., task progress) from the remote agent to the client.
JSON-RPC 2.0: The data exchange format for all requests and responses, providing a standardized structure for remote procedure calls.
Key Data Structures
The protocol defines several core data structures:
1. Agent Card
The Agent Card is a public metadata document (typically JSON) describing a remote agent’s identity, capabilities, skills, endpoint URL, and authentication requirements. It allows client agents to discover and understand how to interact with remote agents.
Key Fields:
name, description, version: Basic agent identification.
provider: Information about the agents provider/organization.
url: The base endpoint URL for the agents A2A service.
documentationUrl: Link to human-readable documentation.
capabilities: Flags indicating support for features like streaming, pushNotifications, stateTransitionHistory.
authentication: Specifies supported authentication schemes (e.g., "bearer", "oauth2") aligned with OpenAPI standards.
defaultInputModes, defaultOutputModes: Default communication modalities (e.g., "text", "data", "audio").
skills: An array describing specific functions the agent can perform, including id, name, description, tags, examples, and supported inputModes/outputModes for each skill.
Example Snippet (Flight Booking Agent Card):
{
"name": "FlightBookingAgent",
"description": "Specialized agent for finding and booking flights",
"url": "https://flights.example.com/agent",
"provider": { "organization": "Travel Services Corp" },
"version": "1.0.0",
"capabilities": { "streaming": true, "pushNotifications": true },
"authentication": { "schemes": ["bearer"] },
"skills": [
{
"id": "flight-search",
"name": "Flight Search",
"description": "Searches for available flights based on criteria",
"inputModes": ["text", "data"],
"outputModes": ["text", "data"]
},
{
"id": "flight-booking",
"name": "Flight Booking",
"description": "Books selected flights",
"inputModes": ["text", "data"],
"outputModes": ["text", "data"]
}
]
}
Agent Card Discovery:
Well-Known Path (Recommended): Hosting the card at https://DOMAIN/.well-known/agent.json allows discovery via DNS.
Curated Registries: Enterprise catalogs or specific registries.
Private APIs: For proprietary agents, cards exchanged via custom APIs.
Securing Agent Cards: Access to Agent Cards, especially those containing sensitive endpoint or capability information, should be protected using standard authentication and authorization mechanisms (e.g., mTLS, registry authentication). Credentials should never be exposed without authentication.
2. Task
The Task is the central unit of work and interaction. It represents a specific job requested by the client agent and processed by the remote agent.
Key Fields:
id: Unique identifier for the task.
sessionId: Optional identifier to group related tasks.
status: The current state of the task (see Task Lifecycle).
artifacts: Outputs generated by the task.
metadata: Optional application-specific data.
Task Lifecycle and States:
Tasks progress through a defined lifecycle:
submitted: Task received but not yet started.
working: Task is actively being processed.
input-required: Agent needs more information from the client to proceed.
completed: Task finished successfully.
canceled: Task terminated (usually by client request).
failed: An error occurred during processing.
unknown: State cannot be determined.
Task Lifecycle Diagram:
There are three main actors in the task lifecycle: the user, the client agent, and the remote agent.
User: The end-user (human or service) that is using an agentic system to accomplish tasks.
Client: The entity (service, agent, application) that is requesting an action from an opaque agent on behalf of the user.
Remote Agent (Server): The opaque (“blackbox”) agent which is the A2A server.

3. Message
Messages encapsulate the content exchanged between agents within a task.
Key Fields:
role: Indicates the sender ("user" for client-originated, "agent" for remote-originated).
parts: An array containing the actual content (see Part).
metadata: Optional application-specific data.
4. Part
Parts represent individual pieces of content within a Message or Artifact. A2A supports multiple part types for rich communication:
TextPart (type: "text"): Contains textual content (text field).
FilePart (type: "file"): Contains file information via a file object (FileContent). The FileContent object includes optional name and mimeType, and requires either bytes (base64 encoded file content) or a uri pointing to the file location.
DataPart (type: "data"): Contains structured data (data field, typically a JSON object).
Each part type can also include optional metadata.
5. Artifact
Artifacts represent the outputs or results produced by a task. An artifact can contain multiple parts.
Key Fields:
name: Identifier for the artifact.
description: Human-readable description.
parts: An array of Parts comprising the artifacts content.
index: Order of the artifact, crucial for chunked delivery.
append: Boolean indicating if this artifact appends to a previous one with the same name.
lastChunk: Boolean indicating if this is the final chunk for this artifact.
metadata: Optional application-specific data.
6. Push Notification Configuration
Used to configure asynchronous updates when direct streaming (SSE) is not feasible or desired.
Key Fields:
url: The endpoint where the remote agent should send notifications.
token: A security token for the notification endpoint.
authentication: Specifies authentication requirements for the notification endpoint.
Push Notification Security: Implementing push notifications requires careful security considerations. The remote agent must verify the notification service’s identity and authenticate itself. The notification URL provided by the client should not be blindly trusted. Recommended security practices include:
* Using asymmetric (e.g., JWT with RSA/ECDSA) or symmetric keys for signing/verifying notification payloads.
* Leveraging OAuth for token-based authentication.
* Implementing replay prevention (e.g., using timestamps like iat in JWT).
* Supporting key rotation (e.g., via JWKS).
* Verifying notification URL ownership via a challenge-response mechanism before use.
Error Handling
A2A uses the standard JSON-RPC 2.0 error object format within responses:
interface ErrorMessage {
code: number; // Numeric error code
message: string; // Human-readable error description
data?: any; // Optional additional error details
}

Clients must be prepared to handle these errors gracefully, potentially retrying, notifying users, or using fallback mechanisms.
Streaming Error Handling: Errors during SSE streaming are sent as specific SSE events containing the JSON-RPC error object, typically terminating the stream. Connection errors require client-side retry logic, potentially using tasks/resubscribe if supported by the agent.
Key Protocol Operations (JSON-RPC Methods)
A2A defines several core methods for task management and communication:
1- tasks/send:
Purpose: Initiates a new task or sends additional input for an existing task (e.g., in the input-required state).
Params (TaskSendParams): Requires id (unique task identifier, must be provided by client) and message (containing role and parts). Optional fields include sessionId, pushNotification (config object), historyLength (integer), and metadata.
2- tasks/get:
Purpose: Retrieves the current status and artifacts of a specific task. Used for polling when streaming is not active.
Params (TaskQueryParams): Requires task id. Optional fields include historyLength (integer) and metadata.
Result: The full Task object including current status, artifacts, etc.
3- tasks/cancel:
Purpose: Requests the cancellation of an ongoing task.
Params (TaskIdParams): Requires task id. Optional metadata.
Result: The Task object reflecting the cancellation status (e.g., state changed to canceled or an error if cancellation failed).
4- tasks/sendSubscribe:
Purpose: Initiates a task and establishes an SSE stream for real-time updates (status changes, artifacts). Preferred method for long-running or interactive tasks.
Params: Similar to tasks/send.
Response: An HTTP response with Content-Type: text/event-stream. Events contain JSON-RPC response objects (result or error).
5- tasks/pushNotification/set:
Purpose: Configures push notification settings for a specific task.
Params: Task id, pushNotificationConfig object.
Result: Confirmation of configuration update.
6- tasks/pushNotification/get:
Purpose: Retrieves the current push notification configuration for a task.
Params (TaskIdParams): Requires task id.
Result: The pushNotificationConfig object associated with the task, or null if not set.
7- tasks/resubscribe:
Purpose: Re-establishes a lost SSE connection for an existing task to resume receiving real-time updates.
Params (TaskQueryParams): Requires task id. Optional historyLength (to potentially replay missed events, though exact behavior is implementation-dependent) and metadata.
Response: An HTTP response with Content-Type: text/event-stream, similar to tasks/sendSubscribe, resuming the stream of updates.
A2A and MCP: Complementary Protocols
A2A is designed to coexist and complement other protocols in the AI ecosystem, most notably Anthropic’s Model Context Protocol (MCP). They serve distinct but related purposes:
MCP: Focuses on connecting a single agent (or language model) to tools and structured data sources. It acts like a plugin system, enhancing an individual agent’s capabilities by giving it access to external functionalities (APIs, databases, etc.) with well-defined inputs and outputs.
A2A: Focuses on agent-to-agent communication. It acts as a networking layer, enabling multiple autonomous agents to collaborate, delegate tasks, and exchange information, often using more natural or unstructured modalities, without necessarily sharing internal state, tools, or context directly.
In essence, while MCP focuses on standardizing how a single agent accesses tools, A2A standardizes how multiple agents communicate and collaborate.
Key differences include:
MCP operates primarily with local context and lacks built-in agent authentication, whereas A2A facilitates multi-agent interactions (potentially involving shared state and task delegation), includes secure communication mechanisms, and allows agents to discover each other’s capabilities.
Tools are primitives with structured inputs/outputs and predictable behavior.
Agents are autonomous applications capable of reasoning, using tools, and interacting to accomplish novel tasks.
Effective AI applications often require both: agents need access to tools (via MCP) to perform specific actions, and they need to collaborate with other agents (via A2A) to solve complex problems.
Integration Pattern:
A common pattern is to model A2A agents as MCP resources. An agent might use MCP to discover and interact with tools, while simultaneously using A2A to communicate with other agents or delegate sub-tasks. The Agent Card can serve as the description for the agent when exposed as an MCP resource.

Enterprise Readiness
A key design goal of A2A is seamless integration with existing enterprise infrastructure and security practices. It models agents as standard HTTP-based applications, relying on established patterns rather than inventing new ones.
Transport Security: HTTPS with modern TLS is mandatory for production.
Server Identity: Verified via standard TLS certificate validation.
Client and User Identity:
A2A itself doesn’t mandate specific identity schemas within its payloads.
Authentication requirements are declared in the Agent Card (e.g., OAuth, API Keys).
Clients negotiate with authentication authorities outside the A2A protocol flow.
Credentials (e.g., bearer tokens) are transmitted via standard HTTP headers (e.g., Authorization), not within A2A JSON payloads.
It’s recommended clients present both their own identity (application identity) and the end-user’s identity (user identity) when applicable.
For multi-identity federation (where an agent needs credentials for downstream systems), the agent can transition to the input-required state, requesting the necessary credentials from the client.
Authentication: Servers authenticate every request based on the schemes published in their Agent Card, using standard HTTP status codes (401, 403) for challenges or rejections.
Authorization: Access control should be enforced based on authenticated identities (both client and user), potentially using role-based or scope-based authorization managed by the agent implementation.
Tracing and Observability: Standard enterprise tools for HTTP request tracing (e.g., OpenTelemetry), logging, and monitoring should be used, leveraging correlation IDs (like the JSON-RPC id or task id) to track interactions across agents.
Example: Travel Planning
A2A enables sophisticated collaboration across various domains. The travel planning scenario serves as a prime example. It’s a multi-agent system for travel planning demonstrates A2A’s strengths:
Travel Coordinator Agent: User interface, orchestrator, aggregates results.
Flight Booking Agent: Finds/books flights.
Hotel Reservation Agent: Finds/books accommodations.
Local Activities Agent: Suggests/books tours, restaurants.
Transportation Agent: Arranges ground transport.
Workflow:
User interacts with the Travel Coordinator.
Coordinator parses the request (e.g., “Plan a week in Paris in June”).
Coordinator uses tasks/send (or tasks/sendSubscribe) to delegate sub-tasks (flight search, hotel search) to specialized agents via A2A.
Specialized agents process tasks, potentially streaming updates (working status, intermediate results).
Agents return final results or request more input (input-required).
Coordinator presents options to the user.
User makes selections.
Coordinator sends booking requests to specialized agents via A2A.
Agents confirm bookings.
Coordinator assembles the final itinerary.
Direct Agent Communication (Optional): The Activities Agent might directly query the Hotel Agent (via A2A) for the booked hotel’s location to provide relevant nearby suggestions.

Current Limitations and Challenges
Despite its potential, A2A is an emerging protocol with areas needing further development:
Documentation Gaps: While foundational, current documentation could benefit from more comprehensive schema references, detailed guides on discovery/onboarding, multi-modality handling specifics (audio/video), and more diverse cross-vendor examples.
Multi-Agent Orchestration: A2A provides the communication layer, but higher-level patterns for managing complex interactions (conflict resolution, cascading failure handling, resource optimization, ensuring consistent outcomes) are still evolving and largely outside the core protocol specification.
Security and Trust: Establishing trust between agents from different providers, preventing malicious agent interactions, managing authentication/authorization across complex chains, and ensuring data privacy across boundaries remain significant challenges as ecosystems grow.
Performance and Scalability: Limited guidance exists on optimizing for high-volume interactions, low latency, resource management in large agent networks, and performance benchmarking.
Economic Models: While agent monetization is possible, standardized mechanisms for pricing, inter-agent transactions, SLAs, and dispute resolution are not defined within the protocol.
Future Directions
A2A provides a good foundation for future advancements in agent collaboration; however, there are several areas that could be improved in my opinion:
1- Enhanced Standardization: Maturation will likely bring more detailed standards for agent capability descriptions, Quality-of-Service (QoS) metrics, common error/recovery patterns, and cross-vendor authentication/identity federation mechanisms.
2- Advanced Orchestration Frameworks: Frameworks built atop A2A could emerge, offering declarative workflow specifications, formal verification methods, dynamic agent discovery/negotiation, top-down and bottom-up planning based on agent capabilities, capabilities and task requirements, and adaptive orchestration based on real-time performance.
3- Agent Marketplaces and Economics: The protocol could be extended (or complemented by other standards) to support agent marketplaces with features like:
Standardized cost/chargeback structures and payment mechanisms in Agent Cards, so that agents can be priced and traded in a marketplace.
Defined Service Level Agreements (SLAs).
Rating/reputation systems.
Automated negotiation and transaction handling.
4- Input Constraints and Validation: Agent Cards could incorporate standardized ways to define input requirements, such as:
JSON Schema definitions for structured data inputs.
Length/size limits for text/file inputs.
Rate limiting information.
Standardized validation error responses.
5- Regulatory and Ethical Frameworks: As autonomous agent interactions become more prevalent and impactful, frameworks addressing transparency, accountability, ethical decision-making, and compliance verification will become increasingly important.
Conclusion
The A2A Protocol represents a crucial step towards enabling seamless collaboration between AI agents, moving beyond isolated systems towards interconnected, cooperative networks. By providing standardized communication patterns built on existing web technologies and focusing on enterprise readiness, A2A facilitates the development of more complex, capable, and scalable AI solutions.
While still evolving and facing challenges related to orchestration, security, and standardization depth, the strong industry backing and clear design principles position A2A as a potentially foundational element of the emerging agentic AI landscape. It provides an essential framework for the transition towards a future where AI agents work together effectively across organizational and technological boundaries.

An open protocol enabling communication and interoperability between opaque agentic applications.
The Agent2Agent (A2A) protocol addresses a critical challenge in the AI landscape: enabling gen AI agents, built on diverse frameworks by different companies running on separate servers, to communicate and collaborate effectively - as agents, not just as tools. A2A aims to provide a common language for agents, fostering a more interconnected, powerful, and innovative AI ecosystem.
With A2A, agents can:
Discover each other's capabilities. Negotiate interaction modalities (text, forms, media). Securely collaborate on long-running tasks. Operate without exposing their internal state, memory, or tools. DeepLearning.AI Course

As AI agents become more prevalent, their ability to interoperate is crucial for building complex, multi-functional applications. A2A aims to:
Break Down Silos: Connect agents across different ecosystems. Enable Complex Collaboration: Allow specialized agents to work together on tasks that a single agent cannot handle alone. Promote Open Standards: Foster a community-driven approach to agent communication, encouraging innovation and broad adoption. Preserve Opacity: Allow agents to collaborate without needing to share internal memory, proprietary logic, or specific tool implementations, enhancing security and protecting intellectual property. Key Features
Standardized Communication: JSON-RPC 2.0 over HTTP(S). Agent Discovery: Via "Agent Cards" detailing capabilities and connection info. Flexible Interaction: Supports synchronous request/response, streaming (SSE), and asynchronous push notifications. Rich Data Exchange: Handles text, files, and structured JSON data. What is Streaming Processing?
The A2A protocol's streaming processing mechanism is specifically designed to handle AI tasks that require long execution times, produce incremental results, or need real-time feedback. Through Server-Sent Events (SSE) technology, clients can receive real-time task progress updates and partial results.
Core Features of Streaming Processing
Feature Description Use Cases Real-time Updates Push task status changes via SSE Long document generation, media stream processing Incremental Results Chunked transmission of large artifacts Large file processing, real-time analysis Connection Management Support for reconnection and state recovery Unstable network environments Event Types Multiple event types for different update needs Status updates, artifact updates Streaming Processing Workflow

{ "capabilities": { "streaming": true } } 2. Event Structure
A2A streaming processing supports three main event types:
Task Events: Represent task status units being processed TaskStatusUpdateEvent: Communicate task lifecycle status changes TaskArtifactUpdateEvent: Deliver newly generated or updated artifacts 💡 Pro Tip Each SSE event's data field contains a complete JSON-RPC 2.0 response object, ensuring compatibility with standard protocols.
3. Reconnection Mechanism

✅ Recommended scenarios for streaming processing:
Long-running tasks requiring real-time progress monitoring Incremental reception of large results Interactive conversations requiring immediate feedback Applications requiring low-latency updates Asynchronous Operations Push Notifications {#async-operations}
Push Notification Mechanism Overview
For extremely long-running tasks (minutes, hours, or even days) or clients unable to maintain persistent connections (such as mobile apps, serverless functions), A2A provides a Webhook-based push notification mechanism.
Push Notification Configuration
PushNotificationConfig Structure

Server-side Security Measures
⚠️ Important Security Reminder Servers should not blindly trust client-provided Webhook URLs and need to implement the following security measures:
URL Validation
Maintain trusted domain whitelist Implement ownership verification mechanisms Use network egress controls Authentication
Bearer Token (OAuth 2.0) API Key authentication HMAC signature verification Mutual TLS (mTLS) Client-side Security Measures
## Client Webhook Security Checklist ✅ Verify server identity (JWT signature, HMAC, etc.) ✅ Check PushNotificationConfig.token ✅ Implement timestamp verification to prevent replay attacks ✅ Use unique IDs (nonce) to prevent duplicate processing ✅ Secure key management and rotation Extension Mechanisms Deep Dive {#extensions}
Extension System Architecture
A2A's extension system allows adding custom functionality on top of the core protocol without breaking basic compatibility. Extensions are identified by URIs and support version management and dependency relationships.
Extension Type Classification
Extension Type Description Example Uses Data Extensions Add structured information only in AgentCard GDPR compliance info, terms of service Profile Extensions Add structure and state requirements to core protocol Medical data encryption, FHIR standards Method Extensions Add entirely new RPC methods Task history search, batch operations Extension Declaration Example
{ "name": "Magic 8-ball", "capabilities": { "extensions": [ { "uri": "https://example.com/ext/konami-code/v1", "description": "Provide cheat codes to unlock new fortunes", "required": false, "params": { "hints": [ "When your sims need extra cash fast", "You might deny it, but we've seen the evidence of those cows." ] } } ] } } Extension Activation Flow
graph TD A[Client requests extension activation] -- B[Add X-A2A-Extensions header] B -- C[Server checks supported extensions] C -- D[Verify extension dependencies] D -- E[Activate compatible extensions] E -- F[Return X-A2A-Extensions response header] F -- G[Execute extension logic] Extension Development Best Practices
Version Management Strategy
## Extension Version Management Standards - Use URI paths containing version numbers: `/ext/my-extension/v1` - Breaking changes must use new URIs - Servers should not automatically downgrade to different versions - Recommend using permanent identifier services (like w3id.org) Packaging and Distribution
# Example: Python server integration from konami_code_extension import CheatCodeHandler from a2a.server import A2AServer, DefaultRequestHandler extension = CheatCodeHandler() extension.add_cheat( code="motherlode", hint="When your sims need extra cash fast" ) request_handler = DefaultRequestHandler( agent_executor=MyAgentExecutor(extension), task_store=InMemoryTaskStore(), extensions=[extension] ) Task Lifecycle Management {#task-lifecycle}
Task State Machine
Tasks in the A2A protocol follow a clear lifecycle state machine, supporting complex workflow management.
graph TD A[Create task] -- B[working] B -- C{Need input?} C --|Yes| D[input-required] C --|No| E{Need authorization?} E --|Yes| F[auth-required] E --|No| G{Task completed?} G --|Success| H[completed] G --|Failed| I[failed] G --|Canceled| J[canceled] D -- K[Receive input] -- B F -- L[Complete authorization] -- B Context and Task Relationships
Role of contextId
Logical Grouping: Organize multiple tasks and independent messages together Context Management: Provide continuous conversation context for LLMs Collaboration Support: Support multi-task collaboration around common goals Task Non-Restart Principle
💡 Design Philosophy Once a task reaches a terminal state, it cannot be restarted. This design brings the following benefits:
Task Immutability: Clients can reliably reference tasks and their states Clear Work Units: Each request, refinement, or follow-up operation becomes an independent task Simplified Implementation: Avoids the complexity of restarting existing tasks Task Refinement and Follow-up Operations
Parallel Follow-up Task Example
Task 1: Book flight to Helsinki (After Task 1 completes) Task 2: Based on Task 1, book hotel Task 3: Based on Task 1, book snowmobile activity (After Task 2 completes, Task 3 still in progress) Task 4: Based on Task 2, add spa service to hotel booking Artifact Reference Mechanism

Practice Description Benefits Minimize required extensions Only mark core functionality as required Maintain client compatibility Complete input validation Validate all extension-related data Improve security and stability Clear documentation Provide detailed specification documentation Promote adoption and correct implementation Version compatibility Handle breaking changes carefully Protect existing integrations Frequently Asked Questions {#faq}
Q: How to choose between streaming processing and push notifications?
A: The choice mainly depends on task characteristics and client capabilities:
Streaming Processing: Suitable for scenarios requiring real-time feedback, short task execution times (minutes), and clients that can maintain connections Push Notifications: Suitable for long-running tasks (hours/days), mobile applications, serverless functions, and other scenarios where long connections cannot be maintained Q: How are extension dependencies managed?
A: Extension dependencies are declared in the extension specification, and clients are responsible for activating extensions and all their required dependencies. If clients don't request required dependencies, servers should reject the request and return appropriate errors.
Q: How to recover after task failure?
A: Once a task reaches a terminal state, it cannot be restarted. When recovery is needed:
Use the same contextId to initiate a new request Reference the failed task through referenceTaskIds Handle error recovery logic in the new task Q: How to ensure push notification reliability?
A: Push notification reliability strategies include:
Implement retry mechanisms and exponential backoff Use message queues to ensure delivery Provide notification status query interfaces Implement client active polling as a fallback Q: How to maintain compatibility during extension version upgrades?
A: Version upgrade strategies:
Non-breaking changes can be updated under the same URI Breaking changes must use new URIs Servers can support multiple versions simultaneously Provide migration guides and transition period support Summary and Next Steps
